{{Short description|Measurement of difference between votes received and seats won}}

The '''Loosemore–Hanby index''' measures [[Proportional representation|disproportionality]] of [[electoral system]]s, how much the principle of [[one person, one vote]] is violated.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Loosemore |first1=John |last2=Hanby |first2=Victor J. |date=October 1971 |title=The Theoretical Limits of Maximum Distortion: Some Analytic Expressions for Electoral Systems |journal=[[British Journal of Political Science]] |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=467–477 |doi=10.1017/S000712340000925X |jstor=193346 |s2cid=155050189}}</ref> It computes the absolute difference between votes cast and seats obtained using the formula:

{{in5}}<math>LH=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n|v_i-s_i|</math>,<br />where
<math>v_i</math> is the vote share and
<math>s_i</math> the seat share of party
<math>i</math>
such that <math>\Sigma_i v_i = \Sigma_i s_i = 1</math>,
and <math>n</math> is the overall number of parties.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cortona |first1=Pietro Grilli di |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A1tNCQg2QKEC |title=Evaluation and Optimization of Electoral Systems |last2=Manzi |first2=Cecilia |last3=Pennisi |first3=Aline |last4=Ricca |first4=Federica |last5=Simeone |first5=Bruno |date=1999 |publisher=[[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|SIAM]] |isbn=978-0-89871-422-7}}</ref>

This index is minimized by the [[largest remainder method|largest remainder (LR) method]] with the [[Hare quota]]. Any apportionment method that minimizes it will always apportion identically to LR-Hare. Other methods, including the widely used [[highest average method|divisor methods]] such as the [[Webster/Sainte-Laguë method]] or the [[D'Hondt method]] minimize the [[Sainte-Laguë Index|Sainte-Laguë index]] instead.

The index is named after John Loosemore and Victor&nbsp;J. Hanby, who first published the formula in 1971 in a paper entitled "The Theoretical Limits of Maximum Distortion: Some Analytic Expressions for Electoral Systems". Along with [[Douglas W. Rae]]'s, the formula is one of the two most cited disproportionality indices.<ref name=grofman>{{cite book
|last      = Grofman
|first     = Bernard
|title     = Elections in Japan, Korea, and Taiwan Under the Single Non-transferable Vote: The Comparative Study of an Embedded Institution
|url       = https://books.google.com/books?id=ry26lbfP16sC
|year      = 1999
|publisher = [[University of Michigan Press]]
|isbn      = 0-472-10909-X
}}
</ref>
Whereas the '''Rae index''' measures the average [[Deviation (statistics)|deviation]], the Loosemore–Hanby index measures the total deviation. [[Michael Gallagher (academic)|Michael Gallagher]] used [[least squares]] to develop the [[Gallagher index]], which takes a middle ground between the Rae and Loosemore–Hanby indices.<ref name=lg>
{{cite book
|last1     = Lijphart
|first1    = Arend
|last2     = Grofman
|first2    = Bernard
|title     = The Evolution of Electoral and Party Systems in the Nordic Countries
|url       = https://books.google.com/books?id=oigZTGYdQb4C
|year      = 2007
|publisher = [[Algora Publishing]]
|isbn      = 978-0-87586-168-5
}}
</ref>

The LH index is related to the [[Hoover index|Schutz index]] of inequality, which is defined as<math display="block">S = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} |e_i - a_i|,</math>where <math>e_i</math> is the expected share of individual <math>i</math> and <math>a_i</math> her allocated share. Under the LH index, parties take the place of individuals, vote shares replace expectation shares, and seat shares allocation shares. The LH index is also related to the [[dissimilarity index|dissimilarity index of segregation]]. All three indexes are special cases of the more general <math>\Delta</math> index of dissimilarity.<ref>
{{cite book
|last     = Agesti
|first    = Alan
|title     = Categorical Data Analysis
|url       = https://books.google.com/books?id=hpEzw4T0sPUC
|year      = 2002
|publisher = Wiley
|isbn      = 0-471-36093-7
}}
</ref> The LH index is related to the amount of [[wasted vote]], which only measures the difference between votes cast and seats obtained for parties which did not obtain any seats. 

The complement of the LH index is called '''Party Total Representativity''',<ref>{{Cite web|title=Voting matters, Issue 10: pp 7-10|url=http://www.votingmatters.org.uk/ISSUE10/P6.HTM|access-date=2021-04-18|website=www.votingmatters.org.uk}}</ref> also called '''Rose index''' R. The Rose index is typically expressed in % and can be calculated by subtracting the LH index from 1:<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://doi.org/10.1016/0261-3794(91)90005-D | doi=10.1016/0261-3794(91)90005-D | title=A note on rose's proportionality index | date=1991 | last1=Fry | first1=Vanessa | last2=McLean | first2=Iain | journal=Electoral Studies | volume=10 | pages=52–59 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

{{in5}}<math>R=1-LH=1-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n|v_i-s_i|</math>.<br />

== Application ==

=== Europe ===
The following table displays a calculation of the Rose Index by [[Dieter Nohlen|Nohlen]] of the most, or second most, recent legislative election in each European country prior to 2009. This calculation ranges from 0-100, with 100 being the most proportional score possible, and 0 the least. Parties which received less than 0.5% of the vote were not included.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Stöver |first1=Philip |title=Elections in Europe: A Data Handbook |last2=Nohlen |first2=Dieter |publisher=Nomos |year=2010 |isbn=9783832956097 |language=English}}</ref>
